attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create 3 image assets from the Create New Asset menu?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image assets might be used in this project? 

❓ How do you rename an asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja notice the white box at the bottom of the editor. They can replace the existing text with a descriptive name for their asset, written in camelCase. This is useful when calling the asset in their code. 

💡 Point out to the ninja what happens when they select a specific asset. On the left side menu, a preview of the asset appears and tells about its properties (type and size). From this side menu, the asset can be edited, duplicated, copied, or deleted.
steps.instructions:
Begin by storing assets to be used in this project! 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, then click the green (+) to add a new asset to My Assets. From the Create New Asset menu, select Image. 


Select an image from the Gallery for a Player sprite. Notice the white box on the bottom of the screen with the name of the image. Replace “myImage” with a descriptive name that will be used in the project code. Click Done to add the image to My Assets.


Repeat this process to create 2 additional image assets, to be used for Enemy and Food sprites. Give each image a descriptive name before clicking Done and returning to My Assets.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create Enemy and Food sprite spawn tile assets and give them descriptive names, like this?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What type of theme might be used in this project? What theme matches the sprite images already in My Assets?

❓ Why is it helpful to design tiles that match the theme of the project?

❓ What type of tile might be used to spawn Enemy and Food sprites?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to consider the theme of their project, as well as the theme of the sprite image assets when creating a custom tile. This tile will be added to a tilemap asset in the next step. 

💡 Remind the ninja to give each tile a descriptive name, written in camelCase. This is useful when calling the asset in their code and matching it to the correct sprite.
steps.instructions:
Design tiles to spawn Enemy and Food sprites on a tilemap! 


Click the green (+) again. From the Create New Asset menu, select Tile. 


Design a tile using the editor tools, or select one from the Gallery, where an Enemy sprite will spawn. Create a tile that will match the theme of the project. Once finished, replace “myTile'' with a descriptive name that will be used in the project code. Click Done to add the tile to My Assets.


Repeat this process to create 1 additional tile asset to spawn a Food sprite. Rename the tile before returning to My Assets.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the Food and Enemy spawn tiles strategically in your tilemap, so that Food and Enemy sprites spawn in different places?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where do tiles created in My Assets appear in the tilemap editor?

❓ How do you add walls to a tilemap?

❓ How many Food or Enemy spawn tiles might be added? How might changing the number of each tile used affect the project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja of the different features of the tilemap editor. When editing a tilemap, the ninja has all of the same paint tools available to them. However, they can also enable walls by selecting the draw walls tool . If a large section of tiles need to have walls set, encourage the ninja to use the fill tool .

💡 Remind the ninja that any custom tile will appear in the My Tiles tab of the tilemap editor. This will be useful for adding the Enemy and Food sprite spawn tile assets onto the tilemap.

💡 Remind the ninja that the default 16 x 16 tilemap is larger than the size of the screen. Prompt the ninja to consider what other code might need to be added for the user to see the entire tilemap on the emulator.
steps.instructions:
Design a 16 x 16 tilemap to use in the project! 


Click the green (+) again. From the Create New Asset menu, select Tilemap. 


In the tilemap editor, use the tiles from the Gallery to design a 16 x 16 tilemap that includes walls. Click My Tiles to add several of the Enemy and Food spawn tiles created in the previous step onto the tilemap design. 


Once finished, replace “level” with a descriptive name that will be used in the project code. Click Done to add the tilemap to My Assets.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use // to add comments to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming assets, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments.
steps.instructions:
Add code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Click the JavaScript tab at the top of the screen to return to the coding editor. Then, add comments for: tilemap set up, sprite set up, sprite overlap events.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type assets and a dot operator, select tilemap from the code completion tool, then type the name of the tilemap asset inside 2 backticks `` in the tilemap parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How can you check the name of the tilemap in My Assets?

❓ What background color and screen effect might match the theme of the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the ninja forgot the name of their tilemap asset, they can open the Assets menu, then select the tilemap to see the preview with the asset name on the left side.

💡Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding a background color or screen effect to the project.
steps.instructions:
Display the tilemap on screen!


Open Scene and drag [set tilemap to (tilemap)] underneath // tilemap set up. 


To access the tilemap created in My Assets, type assets followed by a dot operator before tilemap`` inside the parentheses of the setCurrentTilemap function. Then type the name given to the tilemap inside the 2 backticks ``. 


Then, add a background color and screen effect to complete the project’s background.


Click ▶ to see the tilemap appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the 3 sprite image assets as the image parameters in the sprites.create function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the asset type need to be used in the sprite image parameters?

❓ Where can backticks `` be found on the keyboard?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Explain to the ninja the asset type is important to include because it tells MakeCode what type of image to search for in My Assets. The asset options appear in the code completion tool: image, tile, tilemap, and animation. 

💡 Point out to the ninja that backticks `` can be found to the left of the 1 key on their keyboard.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding sprites to the project.
steps.instructions:
Display the 3 sprite image assets from My Assets on screen!


Add 3 sprites to the project underneath // sprite set up. 


Name each sprite to match the name of the asset created in My Assets, then replace img`...` by typing assets, a dot operator, and image. Type the name given to the sprite’s image asset surrounded by 2 backticks ` `. 


Update the sprite kinds so there are Player, Enemy, and Food sprites.


Click ▶ to see 3 sprite image assets appear on the screen!

steps.hints: 💡 Notice that tilemap coordinates begin at 0 and increase from left to right (column) and top to bottom (row).
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Where might the Player sprite be placed on the tilemap?

❓ Why is it useful to have the camera follow the Player sprite? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that tilemaps use columns and rows to determine the location of specific tiles. Explain that coordinates begin at 0 and increase from left to right (column) and top to bottom (row). The ninja can use their cursor to hover over a specific tile, then find its coordinates in the bottom left corner of the editor.

💡 Explain to the ninja that the 16 x 16 tilemap is larger than the size of the screen. In order to see the Player sprite move around the entire tilemap, the ninja needs to set the camera to follow it.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding the code to move the Player sprite with direction buttons.
steps.instructions:
Place the Player sprite on the tilemap and use the camera to follow the sprite around the screen!


Open Scene and drag [place mySprite on top of (loc)] underneath the Player sprite’s code. Replace mySprite with the Player sprite’s name. Update the tilemap coordinates in the location parameter to place the Player sprite on the tilemap. 


Add code to move the Player sprite around the tilemap with direction buttons.


Then, open Scene and drag [camera follow sprite (mySprite)] underneath. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

scene.cameraFollowSprite(mySprite) 


The cameraFollowSprite function takes 1 parameter: sprite. Replace mySprite with the name of the Player sprite.


Click ▶ then move the Player sprite around the tilemap to notice how the camera follows the sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type the names of the Enemy and Food sprite spawn tile assets inside 2 backticks `` in the tile parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which tiles should the Enemy and Food sprites be placed on in the tilemap?

❓ Where can the names of the tile assets be found?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they have already created custom tiles to spawn Enemy and Food sprite tiles. Encourage them to double check that they have used tile as the asset type in the tile parameter.

💡 If the ninja forgot the name of their tile assets, they can click over to the Assets menu, then select each tile to see the preview with the asset name on the left side.
steps.instructions:
Place Enemy and Food sprites on random spawn tiles on the tilemap!


Open Scene and drag [place (mySprite) on top of random (tile)] underneath both the Enemy and Food sprite’s code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

tiles.placeOnRandomTile(mySprite, img` `)


The placeOnRandomTile function takes 2 parameters: sprite and tile. Replace mySprite with the sprite’s name. Replace img` ` by typing assets, a dot operator, and tile then typing the name of the sprite’s spawn tile asset surrounded by 2 backticks ` `.


Click ▶ to see Enemy and Food sprites placed randomly on one of the spawn tiles on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check the documentation to update the run condition in each for loop and to assign each Enemy sprite a random velocity?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does the run condition control in a for loop? 

❓ How many Enemy and Food sprites might be spawned in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding the code to create  for loops, set a sprite’s velocity, or set it to bounce on walls. 

💡 Prompt the ninja to open their tilemap asset and notice how many of each spawn tile they placed for each sprite. This may help them determine how many Enemy and Food sprites should be created.
steps.instructions:
Spawn additional Enemy and Food sprites in the project!


Open Loops and drag 2 for loops underneath // sprite set up. Cut and paste all of the Enemy sprite’s code into 1 of the for loops. Update the run condition to set how many Enemy sprites will appear on the screen. 


Repeat this process to set how many Food sprites will appear on screen. 


Inside the Enemy sprite’s for loop, add code to assign each sprite a random velocity, and to bounce on the walls of the tilemap. 


Click ▶ to see several Enemy and Food sprites on the tilemap!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you tinker with the arguments in the cameraShake function to customize what happens when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will happen when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite? What will happen when the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite?

❓ What values might be used to set the amplitude and duration parameters in the cameraShake function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to tinker with the values in the cameraShake function. The amplitude parameter determines the strength at which the camera shakes, and the duration parameter determines how long the camera shakes for.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance adding the code to reposition or destroy sprites in the onOverlap events.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps Enemy and Food sprites!


Open Sprites and drag 2 [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) overlaps (otherSprite) of kind (otherKind)] underneath // sprite overlap events. Add code to reposition or destroy one of the sprites on overlap.


Shake the screen when an overlap occurs. Open Scene and drag [camera shake by (4) pixels for (500) ms] inside the event. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

scene.cameraShake(4, 500) 

The cameraShake function takes 2 parameters: amplitude and duration. Tinker with the argument values so that the camera shakes at a reasonable strength and amount of time. 


Click ▶ then notice what happens when the Player sprite overlaps Enemy and Food sprites!

subgroups.title: Shark Attack
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that places different sprites on random tiles of a tilemap.

validationItems.text: Create 3 image assets, 2 tile assets, and 1 tilemap asset.
Display a tilemap asset on screen.
Place the Player sprite on a specific tilemap coordinate and set the camera to follow it.
Spawn multiple Enemy and Food sprites on random tile assets.
Shake the camera when the Player sprite overlaps a sprite of a different kind.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using the Assets menu to create and manage assets in a project, including tilemaps. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: Asset Management
badges.description: Use the Assets menu in the code editor, and use tilemap code and assets in a project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Carefully Curated
badges.description: Use the Assets menu to organize image, tile, and tilemap assets.

badges.title: Art Re-Collecting
badges.description: Access image, tile, and tilemap assets from My Assets in the code editor.

badges.title: Drop a Pin
badges.description: Position sprites on a tilemap using JavaScript.

badges.title: Lights, Camera, Action!
badges.description: Write code to use the camera functions in JavaScript.
